title: Orcas Turn Dead Sunfish Into Exploding Piñatas
summary:
Killer whales are already known for brutal hunting tactics. They slap stingrays, punt seals into the air, and even team up to make waves that knock penguins off ice floes. But new footage shows something even wilder: orcas smashing dead sunfish so hard the fish explode.

Scientists documented this behavior in the Gulf of California in 2024 and 2025. In both cases, one adult orca held a dead sharp-tail sunfish steady while a second orca slammed into it with enough force to pulverize it. The findings were published July 23 in Frontiers in Ethology.

"I was absolutely gobsmacked," said Marianne Nyegaard, a marine biologist at Auckland Museum in New Zealand who was not involved in the study. "I thought it was the coolest thing I had ever seen."

Why would orcas do this? One leading idea is food prep. Sharp-tail sunfish can grow up to 10 feet long — a huge meal for a pod. Smashing one into smaller pieces could make it easier for young orcas to eat. After one of the explosions, a young orca fed on the small bits, noted Francesca Pancaldi, a marine biologist at Mexico's National Polytechnic Institute.

But feeding might not be the only reason. "Killer whales are highly social animals," Pancaldi said. A single activity can provide nutrition, help orcas bond, and teach young whales how to hunt.

Orcas are clever problem-solvers. They ambush blue whales and whale sharks as a team. Nyegaard isn't surprised they found a creative way to deal with sunfish. "Orcas will do all sorts of things," she said. "They are so clever at figuring out how to hunt and deal with a ton of different prey types."

So the next time an orca plays with its food, it might be teaching, sharing, or just having fun.
why_it_matters: Finding out that a wild animal can invent a brand-new trick — and maybe pass it on to its family — changes how scientists judge animal intelligence, and it reminds us how much of the ocean's behaviour nobody has seen yet.

background_read: Orcas — also called killer whales — are actually the largest members of the dolphin family, and they swim in every ocean in family groups called pods.

The Gulf of California (the narrow stretch of sea between Mexico's mainland and the long Baja California peninsula) is famous among biologists for its rich sea life, and orcas have been studied hunting there for years.

Marianne Nyegaard works at the Auckland Museum in New Zealand, where scientists keep and study animal specimens; she specialises in sunfish herself, which is why the exploding-piñata footage stunned her.

Behaviour experts already knew that killer whales pass hunting tricks from one generation to the next — some pods teach calves to slide onto beaches to grab seal pups, others chase fish in tight teams. Those traditions differ from group to group, a little like human customs.
Frontiers in Ethology is a scientific journal — ethology means the study of animal behaviour — where researchers publish new observations only after other scientists check their work.

perspectives.description: For marine biologists, wild footage of an explosion like this is extremely rare, and it adds a brand-new behaviour to the list of clever orca hunting tactics. It suggests killer whales can solve problems in ways people had never imagined.

Some scientists would point out that this was only two sightings, so it is a small sample to build a theory on. Calling it 'teaching' or 'playing' is a guess about what the animals were thinking, and animals may not have human-style motives.
Orca pods around the world already show different hunting cultures, so this may simply be one more example of animals learning from their group rather than from instinct alone.
If researchers keep filming the same pod, they may find out whether the sunfish-smashing trick spreads to other orcas — which would look a lot like a tradition being passed down.
